However, disputes involving ownership and use of reservation lands have led to strained intercultural relations over the years so that meaningful communications and appreciation for each other's culture are frequently lacking. For example, many Indians are involved in litigation against non-Indians over land dealings. In short, the recent historic relationship between Indians and non-Indians has generally been limited to business associations involving leases and non-Indian acquisition of reservation lands. Urban Bear Don't Walk, a recent law school graduate and member of the Crow Tribe has described the situation as "feudalism in reverse," wherein the Indian land owner has, to a degree, become economically dependent upon annual lease rentals from the non-Indian land user. (Oral communication, January 1976). Although residents of a predominately agricultural area, the Indians do not participate to a great degree in the agricultural economy, and a high percentage of their land is in fact leased to non-Indian operatives (BIA, DES 75-2, p. 61). Lack of necessary Indian capital and agricultural management experience may be a factor in this situation.
The majority of the Crow Tribe (80%) speaks English as a second languange. Although there are numerous Crow social and cultural events throughout the year, few non-Indians attend or participate. One exception to this is the annual Crow Indian Fair and Rodeo which draws visitors from throughout the United States. Also, more recently, there have been non-Indian participants in the annual Crow Sun Dance.
